paras: The killing of Ned Roberts was the fatal shooting of a Black levee worker by armed men guarding a dike in East St. Louis, Illinois, on the night of June 9, 1903, a few hours before the Illinois Central embankment broke and flooded much of the city. Wire reports said he had demanded his pay and threatened to break the dike, and that seven men fired on him at once. The shooting was reported as a paragraph inside national flood coverage, and several papers paired it with the killing of a second Black worker, Elijah Anderson, by a guard for refusing to work.

In early June 1903 East St. Louis was fighting rising backwater with crews of men filling and placing sand sacks on its dikes, while guards patrolled the embankments. About a hundred men were on the Illinois Central dike when it gave way thirty minutes after midnight, according to the Washington Times. Roberts, according to the same report, had worked on the dike for several days.

Accounts of what Roberts did before he was shot differ. The most widely reprinted wire paragraph said he was "killed by members of the levee patrol for attempting to tear down a portion of the dike," an act it attributed to anger at not being allowed to draw his pay at once. A second wire version, carried by the Washington Times and the Durango Semi-Weekly Herald, said he demanded his pay and threatened to break the dike unless paid, and that "instantly seven men fired on him" and he fell dead. The Wichita Daily Eagle, which did not name him, said a levee worker demanded his wages "with a threat to cut the water barriers" and was shot dead "without parley."

The St. Louis Palladium, a Black weekly, gave a briefer account: Roberts was shot and killed "while in the act of pulling a sack of dirt" from one of the dikes on Tuesday night. None of the reports named the men who fired or said who had armed or appointed the patrol. The Washington Times and the Durango paper added that Elijah Anderson, another Black worker on the Illinois Central levee, "refused to work" and was killed by a guard the same night.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or any official inquiry into the shooting of Roberts or Anderson was found in the coverage.

White papers carried the shooting on June 10 and 11 as a few lines in long front-page flood dispatches, in Washington, Providence, Marshalltown, Spokane, Walla Walla, Wichita and Durango, among others. They took the guards' side of the story as fact and gave reasons for the killing in the patrol's terms, a threat to the dike or a refusal to work. Headline writers made it the point of the story in some papers: the Durango paper announced "Two Negroes Shot Dead for Refusing to Work on Levee," and the Stark County Democrat ran the wire paragraph under "Death for Deserters." The Spokane Press set the two shootings "in marked contrast" to Theodore Day, "another negro," who drowned while rescuing people with his horse.

Black-press coverage was slight and did not dispute the white wire. The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate reprinted the levee-patrol paragraph under the headline "Negro Shot Dead," in an issue dated June 4, before the flood it describes. The St. Louis Palladium, published across the river, ran a one-sentence item in its "Flood Flotsam" column on June 13 that described Roberts as pulling dirt from the dike rather than threatening it, and gave no reason for the shooting; the same item ran that day in the Grenada Sentinel in Mississippi.

The reports disagree on what Roberts was doing when he was shot: attempting to tear down part of the dike, threatening to break it unless paid, or pulling a sack of dirt from it. All versions come from reports that relay the patrol's account or give no source, and none quotes a witness. Papers also differ on how many Black workers were shot on the levee that night: the levee-patrol paragraph and the Palladium name only Roberts, while the Washington Times, Spokane Press and Durango Herald report two.

reader.title: Killing of Ned Roberts
bases: Roberts, a levee worker, was shot by members of the levee patrol or guards in a dispute over his pay during flood work, and papers paired it with a worker killed for refusing to work (A1, A2, A9).
Two independent wire versions (A1/A4 and A2/A9) and the St. Louis Palladium (A11) agree that Roberts was shot dead on the East St. Louis dike before the break, though they differ on his act.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Two Negroes Shot Dead for Refusing to Work on Levee' (A9) and 'Death for Deserters' (A10) present the shootings as punishment of workers who threatened the dike or quit.
Most papers ran one or two sentences from the wire inside flood stories, giving the patrol's reason as fact.
The Spokane Press set the two shot men 'in marked contrast' to Theodore Day, 'another negro', who drowned rescuing people.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate reprinted the levee-patrol paragraph under 'Negro Shot Dead' without comment.
The St. Louis Palladium's one-line 'Flood Flotsam' item gave no reason for the shooting and described Roberts as pulling dirt from the dike.
